name: BUILD A BEAR WORKSHOP

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: The bull case is stronger than it was a session ago and I have just found the evidence for it myself. If sales per square foot are RISING while revenue falls, the store base is not deteriorating — the company is closing or converting weaker locations and the survivors are more productive, which is exactly what a structurally improved retailer looks like mid-transition. Commercial revenue compounding 23.5% a year toward 7.3% of the mix is capital-light royalty-like income that carries none of the occupancy risk driving the gross-margin decline. On that reading -8% for five years is far too harsh: it applies the operating deleverage of the retail half to the whole company, including the half that is growing 23% and has no leases. At -2% the fair value is well above the price.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Q3 and Q4 fiscal 2026 gross margin against the 54.2% just posted — the same test the prior pass named — and, additionally now, the fiscal 2026 revenue mix: whether commercial plus international franchising continues to climb past 8.3% while total revenue falls. Rising mix share during a down year is the strongest possible version of the structural claim; flat or falling mix share would show the capital-light channel is cyclical too.
devils_advocate.already_visible: The mix evidence is visible through fiscal 2025 and it supports the bull; the fiscal 2026 evidence is not, because the 10-K predates the deterioration and the Q2 release does not break out the mix. So the bull's best evidence is a year stale and the bear's is current. That asymmetry is why I did not move the verdict. The tariff-refund adjustment also removes some of what the prior pass treated as counter-evidence: the $60-68M guide that 'still implies a margin structure nothing like 2019' is $53-61M once the windfall comes out.
devils_advocate.unresolved: I still cannot decompose the post-2020 margin step into structural mix versus pricing cycle in the way the prior pass wanted. The 10-K gives revenue mix and sales per square foot but does not report profitability by channel, so I know commercial is growing and I do NOT know its margin. That was the actual question, and the 10-K does not answer it — which corrects the prior pass's assumption that the segment detail would settle it.

what_changed: This is a second pass on a name last researched 2026-08-31, when the verdict moved cheap to no_edge within a single day. The price has fallen from $30.11 to $28.20. Two genuinely new things. FIRST, I obtained the fiscal 2025 10-K, which the 2026-08-31 pass named as the document it needed and could not open — SEC egress was blocked then and is blocked now, but adhoc-fetch reaches it. It answers the open question in the bull's favour: the capital-light share of revenue has grown steadily, with net retail sales falling from 93.9% to 92.8% to 91.7% of revenue while commercial revenue rose from 5.2% to 6.3% to 7.3% (growing 23.5% in each of the last two years, $25.4M to $31.4M to $38.8M) and international franchising held near 1.0%. Net retail sales per square foot in North America ROSE to $518 from $492 and $495, and in the UK to £735 from £729 and £629. That is a more productive store base plus a growing royalty-and-partner channel — evidence the post-2020 step is at least partly structural rather than purely a collectibles cycle. SECOND, and cutting the other way, the guidance the prior pass leaned on is inflated by an IEEPA tariff refund: the $60-68M full-year pre-tax outlook 'reflects an approximately $13 million IEEPA tariff refund', and EXCLUDING the ~$7M relating to prior-year costs the company guides ADJUSTED pre-tax income of $53-61M. First-half adjusted pre-tax income ex-refund was $28.5M against $34.9M, down 18%, and adjusted EBITDA ex-refund was $35.9M against $41.9M. The 2026-09-09 8-K is a routine $0.23 quarterly dividend declaration.
consensus_case: Build-A-Bear is a 650-location experiential retailer trading at $28.20, down 60% in a year, with a $353.6M market capitalisation and net cash. The market implies FCFF declines about 11% a year for five years. The case for that: fiscal 2026 is the year the five-year record run ends. Q2 revenue fell 7.2% to $115.3M, pre-tax income fell 24% to $11.6M, gross margin fell 340bp on occupancy cost deleverage and increased promotional activity, and the company has now cut its full-year guidance twice, to $500-525M of revenue against $529.8M delivered in fiscal 2025 — an outright decline. Occupancy deleverage in a mall-based fixed-cost format is a compounding mechanism, not a one-off, and the post-2020 margin structure that the bull case rests on has never been tested by a down cycle.
base_case_rationale: I keep the -8% the prior pass reached, but the number now rests on better evidence and on a corrected base. The engine's $37.8M FCFF base is the mean of fiscal 2023-25 and contains no tariff refunds, so it needs no adjustment for that; what it does not know is that fiscal 2026 will land materially below it. Adjusted pre-tax income of $53-61M against roughly $67M in fiscal 2025 is a ~15% decline, which puts forward FCFF nearer $33M than $37.8M. At a $33M base the market implies -8.2% — which is, to within two-tenths of a point, exactly the -8% I underwrite. The two sides genuinely balance. Against the business: revenue declining, gross margin down 340bp with a named structural mechanism, two guidance cuts in one year, a Chief Growth Officer terminated the day before the second. For it: the mix shift to commercial and franchising is real and compounding at 23.5% a year, sales per square foot are rising not falling, the balance sheet carries net cash of about $26M with no debt, and the dividend was maintained. -8% prices a business that shrinks meaningfully from here without pricing a return to the pre-2020 margin structure, which the segment data now argues against.
key_risks: The +203% baseline gap applies a +15.7% five-year revenue CAGR — the record-years run — to a company now guiding revenue DOWN, and should be disregarded

The fiscal 2026 pre-tax guide of $60-68M includes approximately $13M of IEEPA tariff refunds; adjusted for the ~$7M prior-year portion the company's own guide is $53-61M, and first-half adjusted pre-tax income ex-refund fell 18%
Gross margin fell 340bp in Q2 on occupancy cost deleverage and promotional activity, both structural mechanisms in mall retail rather than one-offs
Two guidance cuts in one fiscal year, with pre-tax income down 24% on a 7.2% revenue decline — 3.3x operating deleverage
The channel-margin decomposition that would settle the structural-versus-cyclical question is not disclosed anywhere, including in the 10-K I obtained specifically to answer it
At a $33M base the market implies -8.2% and I underwrite -8.0%; the fair value sits on top of the price, so there is no edge in either direction
$17.6M average daily dollar volume on a $354M company
watch_for: Q3 and Q4 fiscal 2026 gross margin against the 54.2% just posted — recovery toward 57-58% hands the argument to the bull
Whether the fiscal 2026 revenue mix shows commercial plus international franchising continuing past 8.3% of revenue while total revenue falls
Whether the $60-68M pre-tax guide (adjusted $53-61M) is cut a third time
Fiscal 2027 guidance, which will be the first year lapping the tariff refund with no offset
Who replaces the terminated Chief Growth Officer and whether the growth plan is restated
